title: NorthStar's margin squeeze
prompt: NorthStar Components supplies engineered parts to industrial-equipment manufacturers under multi-year contracts. Revenue grew 3% last year, but gross margin fell from 29% to 21%. Management wants to understand the decline and decide how to restore margin without putting strategic customer relationships at risk.
objective: Identify the primary cause of NorthStar's gross-margin decline and recommend a practical response that balances margin recovery with customer retention.

clarificationOptions.label: Which performance measure should we explain?
clarificationOptions.response: Focus on the eight-point decline in gross margin over the last fiscal year.

clarificationOptions.label: Which products and customers are in scope?
clarificationOptions.response: The full components portfolio and all contracted customers are in scope, though contract terms differ by cohort.

clarificationOptions.label: When did the pressure emerge?
clarificationOptions.response: The decline began in the second quarter, shortly after key commodity and freight costs accelerated.

clarificationOptions.label: Did NorthStar open or close any factories?
clarificationOptions.response: The factory footprint was unchanged and is not management's immediate concern.

facts.text: Shipment volume grew 4%, supported by stable demand from major customers.
Realized price per unit declined about 1% because most contracts did not reprice during the year.
Raw-material, energy, and inbound-freight cost per unit rose 14%.
Steel and specialty-resin purchases account for most of the increase in unit input cost.
Direct labor cost per unit rose 2%, below the rate of revenue growth.
Seventy percent of revenue is governed by contracts that permit price resets only at annual renewal.
The annual-reset contracts absorbed higher input costs for an average of eight months before repricing.
Contracts with quarterly input-cost indexing retained a 27% gross margin, versus 18% for annual-reset contracts.
NorthStar's five largest customers represent 46% of revenue, making abrupt blanket repricing risky.
Contracts representing 38% of revenue renew within the next six months.

investigationNodes.label: Understand revenue performance
investigationNodes.interviewerResponse: Revenue grew 3%, so the problem is margin compression rather than a sales decline.

investigationNodes.label: Check shipment volume
investigationNodes.interviewerResponse: Shipment volume grew 4%. Demand remained stable and does not explain the margin decline.

investigationNodes.label: Inspect realized pricing
investigationNodes.interviewerResponse: Realized price per unit slipped 1% because much of the contract base did not reprice during the year.

investigationNodes.label: Break down unit costs
investigationNodes.interviewerResponse: Input costs rose sharply while direct labor remained comparatively stable. The cost bridge is now available.

investigationNodes.label: Inspect direct labor
investigationNodes.interviewerResponse: Direct labor cost per unit rose only 2%, so labor is not the source of the eight-point margin decline.

investigationNodes.label: Inspect material and freight inputs
investigationNodes.interviewerResponse: Steel and specialty resin drove most of a 14% increase in input cost per unit.

investigationNodes.label: Review customer contract terms
investigationNodes.interviewerResponse: Seventy percent of revenue can reprice only at annual renewal, while the remaining contracts use more frequent mechanisms.

investigationNodes.label: Assess customer concentration
investigationNodes.interviewerResponse: The five largest customers contribute 46% of revenue, so NorthStar should avoid an abrupt one-size-fits-all response.

investigationNodes.label: Compare repricing mechanisms
investigationNodes.interviewerResponse: Annual-reset contracts carried inflated costs for an average of eight months and earned substantially lower margins. The contract-cohort exhibit is now available.

investigationNodes.label: Map upcoming renewals
investigationNodes.interviewerResponse: Contracts covering 38% of revenue renew in the next six months, creating a near-term window for targeted changes.

insights.label: Steel, resin, energy, and freight account for most of the unit-cost increase.
Direct labor accounts for most of the unit-cost increase.
Longer repricing lag coincides with materially lower gross margin.
Indexed contracts have the weaker margin outcome.

decisions.label: Use upcoming renewals to add input-cost indexing and targeted interim surcharges, prioritizing exposed contracts while negotiating with strategic customers.
Apply an immediate uniform price increase to every customer regardless of contract terms.
Reduce direct-labor staffing across all plants.

risks.label: Strategic customers may resist indexed pricing or interim surcharges.
Input costs may fall after new pricing terms are agreed.
Negotiations may extend beyond planned renewal dates.

nextSteps.label: Pilot indexed terms with the next group of renewing contracts and track retention and margin recovery.
Send the same immediate increase notice to every customer.
Begin a network-wide workforce reduction review.

efficientPaths.label: Trace input inflation before testing commercial recovery
Trace pricing mechanics before confirming the cost shock
